page: Microsoft Azure E32-16ds_v6 is a memory-optimized virtual machine engineered with a high memory-to-vCPU ratio. Built upon Microsoft Hyper-V, this configuration features a constrained vCPU profile within the 32 vCPU chassis size, allocating 16 dedicated vCPUs mapped to 8 physical cores across two threads per core. The compute hardware is driven by an Intel Xeon 8573C processor running up to 4.2 GHz on the x86_64 architecture, supported by 48 KB of L1 data cache per core, 2 MB of L2 cache per core, and a sizable 260 MB L3 cache. It incorporates advanced vector and matrix instruction extensions including AVX-512, AMX-INT8, and AMX-TILE. It does not include a GPU, but comes bundled with 1888 GB of local NVMe SSD storage.

The memory subsystem is configured with 256.0 GB of RAM, providing a substantial 16.0 GB of memory per core (1:16 vCPU-to-RAM ratio). Benchmark results reflect strong single-core capabilities, achieving 2112.0 points in Geekbench single-core, alongside 2701.0 in Geekbench text processing, placing them in the top 25%. Multi-core throughput remains in the average tier with 13078.0 in Geekbench multi-core and 26677.0 in PassMark CPU score. Memory bandwidth reaches 120.69 GB/sec for large uncached reads and 67.63 GB/sec for uncached writes. Small model LLM text generation shows top-tier throughput at 373.31 tokens/sec, while larger models yield standard CPU inference rates. Redis operations achieve 22.61 million SET operations per second.

Cost efficiency on this instance stems from constrained core licensing. By presenting 16 active vCPUs against the physical resources and 256.0 GB memory footprint of an E32 class chassis, database engines and software licensed per core can access double the RAM allocation per vCPU without incurring software licensing fees for 32 cores. The addition of 1888 GB local NVMe storage provides fast temporary storage without requiring extra remote disks.

The Azure E32-16ds_v6 is specifically fitted for memory-intensive relational databases, in-memory caching platforms such as Redis, heavy analytical processing, and enterprise workloads that require high RAM density per compute core alongside fast scratch disk performance.
